title: Cumulative final review candidate: proteins, enzymes and integrated metabolism

questions.prompt: Protein structure and binding. A fictional 1:1 binding assay uses free ligand at 12 µM and a measured Kd of 4 µM. Use θ = [L]/(Kd + [L]).

response_fields.prompt: Calculate fractional occupancy. Report a fraction from 0 to 1.
At the same temperature and model, which measured change indicates higher affinity?
options: A lower Kd.
A higher Kd.
A larger total protein concentration alone.

questions.prompt: Fit the control and inhibitor initial-rate series to v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) by minimizing squared rate residuals. The enzyme concentration is matched between conditions.

response_fields.prompt: Estimate the apparent Km for the inhibitor series from the observations.
The fitted Vmax is unchanged while apparent Km increases. Which simple inhibition pattern is consistent with this observation?
options: Pure noncompetitive inhibition with unchanged apparent Km.
Competitive inhibition.
Irreversible loss of all active enzyme.

questions.prompt: Purification and recovery. The CSV reports a crude preparation and a later fraction from the same synthetic purification. Compute yield relative to the crude activity and specific-activity enrichment relative to crude.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate recovery of total activity in the later fraction as a percentage of crude activity.
Calculate the fold enrichment in specific activity (activity per mass) relative to crude.

questions.prompt: Free energy and coupling. An isolated synthetic reaction has ΔG = +12 kJ/mol. It is coupled 1:1 to a reaction with ΔG = -20 kJ/mol under the same conditions.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate ΔG for one coupled event.
Which statement distinguishes reaction coupling from catalysis?
options: A catalyst must change the equilibrium constant to make coupling possible.
A favorable coupled ΔG proves every individual reaction is favorable on its own.
The negative summed ΔG favors the coupled forward process; a catalyst changes rate, not the net ΔG for the stated initial and final states.

questions.prompt: Glycolysis and redox. In a synthetic anaerobic preparation, 1 mol glucose is converted completely to 2 mol lactate. Use the standard net glycolytic ATP yield stated in the lesson.

response_fields.prompt: How many mol net ATP are formed per mol glucose under this boundary?
How does lactate dehydrogenase support continued glycolysis?
options: It regenerates NAD+ by transferring reducing equivalents from NADH to pyruvate.
It produces oxygen for the respiratory chain.
It converts NADPH directly into ATP.

questions.prompt: Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Two mol acetyl-CoA pass through the citric-acid cycle. Use 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP per acetyl-CoA, with P/O values 2.5 and 1.5. Exclude transport and upstream activation costs.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the total ATP equivalents from the stated cycle products and P/O values; report the amount in mol.
In oxidative phosphorylation, what is oxygen’s role?
options: It donates electrons to NADH at complex I.
It is the terminal electron acceptor at the end of the respiratory chain.
It directly phosphorylates ADP in the matrix.

questions.prompt: Glycogen and pentose phosphate pathway. Three mol glucose 6-phosphate enter the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway. The separate glycogen statement concerns phosphorylase action at a non-reducing end.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the mol of NADPH generated if all three mol glucose 6-phosphate complete one oxidative pass.
What is the immediate product released by glycogen phosphorylase during chain shortening?
options: Free glucose from every α-1,4-linked residue.
UDP-glucose from the glycogen particle.
Glucose 1-phosphate from an α-1,4-linked residue.

questions.prompt: Fatty-acid oxidation and ketone bodies. For palmitate, use 7 cycles yielding 7 NADH and 7 FADH2, 8 acetyl-CoA, 10 ATP equivalents per acetyl-CoA in the citric-acid cycle, P/O values 2.5/1.5, and an activation cost of 2 ATP equivalents.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the net ATP-equivalent yield under the stated convention; report the amount in mol.
Why does liver export ketone bodies rather than carry out canonical ketone oxidation itself?
options: Hepatocytes lack the SCOT activity required for canonical ketolysis.
Hepatocytes cannot synthesize acetyl-CoA.
Ketone bodies cannot enter any extrahepatic tissue.

questions.prompt: Fatty-acid synthesis and neutral-lipid storage. For palmitate synthesis, start from cytosolic acetyl-CoA and exclude citrate-shuttle costs. For the separate TAG item, assume complete hydrolysis.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate how many mol NADPH are consumed per mol palmitate synthesized.
Calculate how many mol fatty acids are released by complete hydrolysis of 4 mol TAG.

questions.prompt: Amino-acid nitrogen and urea cycle. Five mol nitrogen atoms are available for complete conversion to urea. Use two nitrogen atoms per urea, 3 ATP molecules per urea and 4 high-energy phosphate equivalents per urea.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the maximum mol of urea from the available nitrogen atoms.
Calculate the amount of high-energy phosphate equivalents consumed, in mol.

questions.prompt: Cholesterol feedback and lipoprotein transport. A synthetic hepatocyte has low endoplasmic-reticulum cholesterol. A separate circulating LDL particle bears ApoB-100.

response_fields.prompt: Which transcriptional response is expected in a simplified low-sterol model?
options: SREBP2 is permanently degraded and LDL receptor expression must fall.
SREBP2 processing increases, raising expression of HMG-CoA reductase and LDL receptor.
ApoC-II is converted into HMG-CoA reductase.

response_fields.prompt: Which particle feature supports LDL-receptor recognition?
options: ApoC-II on HDL.
ApoB-48 on hepatic VLDL.
ApoB-100 on LDL.

questions.prompt: Nucleotide synthesis and salvage. A nucleotide synthesis preparation compares purine and pyrimidine assembly order and uses a PRPP-dependent salvage reaction.

response_fields.prompt: Which statement describes de novo purine synthesis?
options: The purine ring is built stepwise on PRPP to form IMP.
The complete purine ring is assembled as a free base before PRPP is attached.
The purine ring is formed from orotate.

response_fields.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: HGPRT converts dUMP to dTMP; ribonucleotide reductase attaches orotate to PRPP.
HGPRT uses PRPP to salvage hypoxanthine to IMP; ribonucleotide reductase converts NDP to dNDP.
Purine salvage rebuilds the entire base ring at no energetic cost.

questions.prompt: Protein purification lab. Interpret a proposed sequence of synthetic fractionation steps and distinguish enrichment from homogeneity.

response_fields.prompt: After a charge-based ion-exchange step, which method adds an orthogonal size-based separation property?
options: A repeat of the same ion-exchange condition.
A calculation of specific activity alone.
Size-exclusion chromatography.

response_fields.prompt: What can a rise in specific activity establish without additional evidence?
options: It supports enrichment under comparable assay conditions, but it does not prove homogeneity.
It proves every contaminant has been removed.
It proves all target protein is active.

questions.prompt: Use the synthetic hepatic cholesterol flux ledger and keep cellular and plasma pools distinct.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate net hepatocyte cholesterol-pool change (synthesis + LDLR uptake − bile-acid conversion − VLDL export). Report mg/h to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is supported by these rates alone?
options: The modelled cellular cholesterol pool rises at the calculated rate; this alone does not determine circulating LDL concentration.
Plasma LDL must fall at the same rate as hepatocyte cholesterol uptake.
The whole-body cholesterol pool is balanced because the listed rates are nonzero.

questions.prompt: Analyze this separate synthetic purine-supply scenario: 5 mol IMP are synthesized de novo and 4 mol hypoxanthine are salvaged to IMP; 3 mol of the resulting IMP pool become AMP and 2 mol become GMP. Count PRPP used by the two supply routes and ATP/GTP used at these branch steps only.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate total PRPP consumption across the two stated routes. Report mol to three significant figures.
Which branch-step nucleotide ledger follows for the stated AMP and GMP products?
options: 3 mol GTP and 2 mol ATP
3 mol ATP and 2 mol GTP
5 mol ATP and no GTP

questions.prompt: Analyze this separate synthetic ATP-pool ledger. Calculate net amount change from the stipulated synthesis and use rates, then bound the interpretation to the stated pool balance.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate net ATP-pool amount change (synthesis − utilization). Report the signed rate in µmol/min to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is supported by this synthetic rate balance?
options: Net ATP-pool amount increases by +15 µmol/min; this alone gives no concentration or pathway-flux estimate.
Synthesis and use are equal, so ATP turnover is zero.
The respiratory chain must produce the same amount of ATP in every cell.

questions.prompt: Use the supplied synthetic glycolytic input and the lesson accounting boundary. Then interpret an uncoupled mitochondrial preparation supplied with oxidizable NADH.

response_fields.prompt: Which set describes the immediate glycolytic products from the stated glucose input, including the carbon product and net energy/redox carriers?
options: 6 mol pyruvate, 6 mol net ATP and 6 mol NADH; glucose carbon remains in pyruvate at this boundary.
6 mol pyruvate, 12 mol net ATP and no NADH.
3 mol pyruvate, 6 mol ATP and 6 mol oxygen.

response_fields.prompt: What can happen when a protonophore dissipates the gradient in the supplied mitochondrial preparation?
options: Electron transport must stop immediately, while ATP synthesis rises.
Oxygen use directly measures ATP production, so both outputs must change in lockstep.
ATP synthesis falls while electron transport and oxygen use can continue under the stated preparation conditions.

questions.prompt: Use the synthetic extrahepatic oxidation assumptions in case 18 to calculate conditional ATP-equivalents from acetoacetate. Then interpret the cited mouse liver/primary-hepatocyte isotope evidence within its pathway boundary.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate conditional ATP-equivalents from the supplied acetoacetate amount. Report mmol ATP-equivalents as mmol to three significant figures.
Which conclusion is supported by the cited mouse liver and primary-hepatocyte study?
options: It supports SCOT-independent anabolic use of ketone-derived carbon in lipid synthesis; it does not establish canonical SCOT-dependent ketolysis or hepatic ATP yield.
It proves all human hepatocytes oxidize ketones through SCOT to produce ATP.
Ketone-carbon labeling in lipids demonstrates that SCOT was required for the observed anabolic fate.

questions.prompt: Use the synthetic citrate isotopologue fractions in case 19. For this item, define labeled citrate as the sum of the M+2 and M+3 fractions.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the change in labeled citrate fraction (late − early). Report a fraction from 0 to 1 to three significant figures.
Which conclusion is supported by this two-time-point labeling comparison alone?
options: The 0.40 increase directly measures a 40% increase in net TCA-cycle flux.
The labeled fraction rises by 0.40, but enrichment alone does not quantify pathway flux.
The 0.40 increase proves a net flux of 0.40 mmol/min through the TCA cycle.

questions.prompt: In the stated mammalian liver model, form 1 mol glucose from two pyruvate. Use the lesson accounting boundary for gluconeogenesis.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the total ATP plus GTP molecules consumed per mol glucose. Report mol ATP + GTP per mol glucose to three significant figures.
Which complete statement about the cofactor cost and even-chain fatty-acid carbon is supported?
options: The pathway uses 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH per glucose, and acetyl-CoA from even-chain fatty acids can yield net glucose by reversing pyruvate dehydrogenase.
The pathway uses 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH per glucose; even-chain fatty-acid acetyl-CoA cannot supply net glucose in mammals.
The pathway uses 6 ATP and no GTP per glucose, and even-chain fatty-acid chains enter gluconeogenesis directly as glucose.

questions.prompt: Use the supplied synthetic TCA-intermediate balance and compare the stated NADH/NAD+ and ATP/ADP ratios with their matched references. Keep a pool-balance calculation separate from pathway-flux inference.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate anaplerotic replenishment minus cataplerotic withdrawal. Report the signed net pool-change rate in mmol/min to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is supported by the synthetic rates and ratios?
options: The pool accumulation rate exactly equals TCA-cycle oxidation flux, so oxidation increased by 0.50 mmol/min.
Elevated ATP/ADP necessarily means greater energy demand, and elevated NADH/NAD+ cannot constrain cycle throughput.
The modeled intermediate pool rises by 0.50 mmol/min; elevated NADH/NAD+ and ATP/ADP are consistent with redox or lower-demand constraints, but these measurements do not quantify TCA-cycle flux.

questions.prompt: Use the matched synthetic glycolysis observations in case 22. ATP and AMP are the stated PFK-1 effectors; fructose-6-phosphate is a measured pool, while glucose uptake and lactate appearance are measured rates.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the increase in glucose uptake flux (energy-stress condition minus control). Report mmol/(L·h) to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is supported by the matched synthetic observations?
options: The lower fructose-6-phosphate pool proves glucose-to-lactate flux fell, and AMP inhibits PFK-1.
The fructose-6-phosphate pool fell, which by itself proves pathway flux increased; rate measurements are unnecessary.
Lower ATP and higher AMP favor PFK-1 activity in this model; the smaller fructose-6-phosphate pool alone does not specify flux, while measured glucose uptake and lactate appearance both rise.

questions.prompt: A fictional homotetramer contains four folded polypeptide chains. A Gly→Asp substitution is introduced into each chain. No downstream structural change is directly measured.

response_fields.prompt: Which structural level is directly changed by the amino-acid substitution?
options: Quaternary structure, because a substitution always changes subunit association.
Primary structure: the amino-acid sequence changes; effects on folding or assembly need separate evidence.
Tertiary structure, because residue identity directly proves a new three-dimensional fold.

response_fields.prompt: If the native tetramer separates into four still-folded monomers, which level is directly lost?
options: Secondary structure: the local alpha helices and beta sheets in each chain.
Tertiary structure: the three-dimensional fold within each chain.
Quaternary structure: the association among multiple polypeptide subunits.

questions.prompt: Use the stated simplified standard-potential pair for electron transfer from reduced cytochrome c (donor E°′ = +0.220 V) to oxygen/water (acceptor E°′ = +0.815 V). Take n = 1 electron per mole of reaction and F = 96.485 kJ/(V·mol).

response_fields.prompt: Calculate ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′ for one mole of electrons transferred. Report kJ/mol to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is supported by the calculated standard free-energy change?
options: The positive ΔE°′ makes ΔG°′ positive, so electron transfer requires ATP hydrolysis and ATP synthase uses electrons directly.
The negative ΔG°′ indicates exergonic electron transfer; respiratory-chain steps can conserve part of the released energy in a proton gradient, which drives ATP synthase.
The oxygen acceptor has a lower reduction potential than the donor, so the proton gradient is unrelated to ATP synthesis.

questions.prompt: A fictional 1:1 binding assay has total receptor R_T = 20 nM, total ligand L_T = 30 nM and K_d = 5 nM. Use the exact equilibrium mass-balance solution for the bound complex.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate [RL] from the exact quadratic solution. Report nM to three significant figures.
Which comparison and approximation rule are supported by these totals?
options: The hyperbolic equation is exact whenever total ligand is known, regardless of receptor concentration.
Because K_d is the free ligand concentration at half occupancy, total ligand can always be substituted for free ligand.
Using total ligand as free ligand predicts about 17.1 nM complex, above the exact 15.0 nM; the hyperbolic approximation is safer when R_T is much smaller than K_d.

questions.prompt: Use the synthetic coupled and uncoupled oxygen-uptake observations in case 26. At this accounting boundary, the listed P/O ratio is oxidative ATP produced per O₂; other ATP sources are excluded.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the oxidative ATP-production rate implied by the uncoupled oxygen uptake and P/O ratio. Report mmol ATP/min to three significant figures.
Which comparison is supported by these observations?
options: Oxygen uptake rises from 12.0 to 15.0 mmol/min, so ATP turnover must also rise 25% and P/O is unchanged.
The uncoupler stops oxygen consumption completely, so oxidative ATP production is zero.
Implied oxidative ATP production falls from 60 to 45 mmol/min despite higher oxygen use because P/O falls; oxygen uptake alone does not specify ATP turnover without the coupling yield.

questions.prompt: A synthetic complete pathway has four flux-control coefficients. Measured values are C₁ = 0.30, C₂ = 0.20 and C₃ = 0.35. Use the summation theorem; then estimate the response to a small 20% decrease in enzyme 2.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate C₄. Report the dimensionless coefficient to three significant figures.
What is the predicted fractional change in pathway flux for the stated small enzyme-2 decrease?
options: Flux falls by about 20%, because every enzyme change transfers one-for-one to pathway flux.
Flux falls by about 4%, because ΔJ/J ≈ C₂(ΔE₂/E₂) = 0.20 × (−20%).
Flux rises by about 4%, because the remaining control coefficients sum to more than one.

questions.prompt: In this synthetic matched culture, pH is fixed and lactate dehydrogenase is treated as near-equilibrium. The medium contains 50% uniformly 13C-labeled glucose. At baseline, lactate is 1.00 mM, pyruvate is 0.100 mM and lactate is 35% M+3. After a respiratory-chain inhibitor, lactate is 4.00 mM, pyruvate is 0.100 mM and lactate is 48% M+3. Estimate the fraction of post-inhibitor lactate derived from medium glucose, then interpret the redox and tracer readouts.

response_fields.prompt: Divide the post-inhibitor lactate M+3 fraction by the fraction of medium glucose labeled. Report the estimated fraction to three significant figures.
Which conclusion is best supported by the paired measurements?
options: The lactate/pyruvate ratio rises from 10 to 40, consistent at fixed pH with a fourfold shift in the LDH-linked cytosolic redox ratio toward NADH; 0.48/0.50 = 0.960 estimates the fraction of lactate from medium glucose, but this source fraction alone is not a production rate.
The ratio proves the respiratory chain is blocked, and the tracer shows the lactate production rate rose by 96%.
Exactly 48% of lactate came from medium glucose because 48% is M+3; the higher lactate/pyruvate ratio indicates a more oxidized cytosol.

questions.prompt: A synthetic matched-cell model has an ATP demand of 6.40 mmol/(L·h). If oxidative phosphorylation is fully blocked, assume glycolysis supplies all ATP at 2.00 mol ATP per mol glucose and forms 2.00 mol lactate per mol glucose. The same model reports oxygen uptake of 1.08 mmol/(L·h) at baseline, 0.05 during respiratory-chain inhibition and 0.95 during a primary glycolytic defect when alternate fuel supports mitochondrial respiration. Calculate the glucose uptake required during the complete block, then interpret which oxygen pattern distinguishes the modeled explanations.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the glucose uptake needed to meet the ATP demand after the complete oxidative-phosphorylation block. Report in mmol/(L·h) to three significant figures.
Which interpretation correctly combines glycolytic output and the oxygen-consumption evidence?
options: Glucose uptake must be 6.40/2.00 = 3.20 mmol/(L·h), giving 6.40 mmol/(L·h) lactate; oxygen uptake falls from 1.08 to 0.05 with chain inhibition but remains near baseline at 0.95 for the glycolytic defect when alternate fuel supports mitochondria. This oxygen pattern distinguishes the modeled cases, with a second independent readout useful for corroboration.
Glucose uptake must be 3.20 mmol/(L·h) and lactate output 6.40 mmol/(L·h), but 0.05 oxygen uptake supports a primary glycolytic defect while 0.95 supports respiratory-chain inhibition.
Glucose uptake must be 0.20 mmol/(L·h), giving 0.40 mmol/(L·h) lactate; either defect should reduce oxygen uptake to the same value.

questions.prompt: In a synthetic first-order protein-turnover model, an enzyme has an 18.0 h half-life. Its synthesis rate changes to a new constant at time zero, starting from the old steady-state amount. Calculate the time required to complete 90.0% of the transition to the new steady-state amount. Then identify the typical time scales of allosteric control, covalent modification and enzyme-abundance change.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the time to complete 90.0% of the adjustment. Report in hours to three significant figures.
Which statement correctly matches the regulatory layers to their typical time scales?
options: Allosteric effectors can alter activity within seconds, covalent modification often acts over seconds to minutes, and a change in enzyme abundance follows expression and protein turnover over hours to days; a 90% adjustment in this model takes about 59.8 h.
Enzyme abundance changes within seconds, while allosteric effectors require hours to days; the 90% adjustment time is about 5.98 h.
Covalent modification takes days to weeks, enzyme abundance changes in seconds, and 90% adjustment takes 18.0 h.

questions.prompt: Use the Hill equation Y = P^n/(P50^n + P^n) with the synthetic carrier parameters in the data table. Calculate the hemoglobin-like carrier’s fraction of capacity unloaded between lung oxygen pressure and resting-tissue oxygen pressure. Then compare it with the non-cooperative myoglobin-like carrier and interpret the Hill coefficient.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate Y_lung − Y_tissue for the hemoglobin-like carrier. Report the fraction to three significant figures.
Which interpretation of the paired carriers is correct?
options: Hemoglobin unloads about 0.208 of capacity (0.978−0.770), while the myoglobin-like carrier unloads about 0.0382; cooperativity makes the hemoglobin curve steeper across this pressure range. The Hill coefficient describes empirical steepness, not the number of binding sites.
The myoglobin-like carrier unloads more because its P50 is lower, and the Hill coefficient gives the exact number of oxygen-binding sites.
Both carriers unload the same fraction because their saturations at 100 mmHg are similar; cooperativity changes affinity only at zero oxygen.

questions.prompt: A synthetic two-step pathway has first-order rates v1 = k1S and v2 = k2A, with S held constant and v1 = v2 at steady state. Compare the enzyme-1-doubled and enzyme-2-halved conditions in the data table. Calculate the higher-minus-lower steady-state flux, then interpret why their intermediate pools do not identify the flux.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate J_enzyme1-doubled − J_enzyme2-halved. Report in mM/min to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is supported by the steady-state model?
options: Both perturbations produce A_ss = 8 mM, but doubling enzyme 1 gives J = k1S = k2A = 4 mM/min, while halving enzyme 2 gives J = 2 mM/min. The same pool can accompany different fluxes; the rate constants or a direct rate measurement are needed to distinguish them.
Both perturbations produce A_ss = 8 mM, so both must have the same flux regardless of k1S or k2.
Halving enzyme 2 doubles the pool and therefore doubles flux to 4 mM/min; doubling enzyme 1 changes the pool but not flux.

questions.prompt: A synthetic short peptide has three Lys side chains (pKa 10.5), two Asp side chains (pKa 4.1), one His side chain (pKa 6.0), an N-terminus (pKa 8.0) and a C-terminus (pKa 3.5). At pH 7.40, assume independent titratable groups. Use f(BH+) = 1/(1+10^(pH−pKa)) for basic groups and f(A−) = 1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)) for acidic groups. Calculate the expected net charge and choose the correct protonation bookkeeping.

response_fields.prompt: Sum the expected fractional charges. Report the net charge in elementary-charge units (dimensionless unit 1) to three significant figures.
Which calculation and interpretation are correct?
options: Use the base protonated fraction for Lys, His and the N-terminus and the acid deprotonated fraction for Asp and the C-terminus. The independent-group sum is about +0.836 elementary charges; fractional values are ensemble averages, and real protein pKa values can shift in a folded environment.
Use the acid deprotonated formula for every group; because pH 7.40 exceeds most pKa values, the peptide is strongly negative.
Treat each group as fully charged with no fractional protonation; this gives the exact net charge, and the pKa values cannot change inside a protein.

questions.prompt: The data table gives synthetic typical pKa values for alanine, glutamate and lysine. For alanine, identify the two pKa values that bracket the neutral zwitterion and calculate its isoelectric point. Then select the rule that correctly chooses pKa values for amino acids with acidic and basic ionizable side chains.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the alanine pI from the two pKa values that bracket the neutral form. Report to three significant figures.
Which pKa-bracketing rule is correct for alanine, glutamate and lysine?
options: Alanine has no ionizable side chain, so its neutral zwitterion is bracketed by pKa 2.34 and 9.69 (pI 6.015). Glutamate uses its two carboxyl pKas (2.20 and 4.25; pI 3.225), while lysine uses its two amino-group pKas (8.95 and 10.53; pI 9.74).
For each amino acid, average the lowest and highest pKa regardless of where the neutral form lies; glutamate and lysine then both have pI values near 6.
Use only the side-chain pKa for every amino acid; alanine has no pI because it has no ionizable side chain.

questions.prompt: A synthetic protein model has pI ≈ 9.5 and net charges of +1.9 at pH 7.4 and +4.1 at pH 6.0. Calculate the charge change on acidification from pH 7.4 to pH 6.0. Then predict the sign of the net charge and the direction of migration and ion-exchange binding at pH 8.0 and pH 10.0.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate Q(pH 6.0) − Q(pH 7.4), in elementary-charge units. Report the dimensionless value to three significant figures.
Which pH-dependent charge, migration and resin-binding interpretation is correct?
options: Acidifying from pH 7.4 to 6.0 raises the modeled net charge by +2.2 elementary-charge units. At pH 8.0 (below pI) the protein is net positive, migrates toward the negative electrode and binds a cation exchanger; at pH 10.0 (above pI) it is net negative, migrates toward the positive electrode and binds an anion exchanger.
Acidifying lowers net charge by 2.2 units. Below pI the protein is negative and binds a cation exchanger; above pI it is positive and binds an anion exchanger.
At the pI the protein has no ionized groups, so it cannot bind either resin; moving above or below pI does not change migration direction.

questions.prompt: Two synthetic enzymes have the matched initial-rate parameters in the data table and equal active enzyme concentrations. Calculate enzyme B’s catalytic efficiency after converting Km from micromolar to molar. Then compare the expected relative rates at 1 μM substrate and near saturation at 1000 μM, and state what catalytic efficiency does not measure.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate kcat/Km for enzyme B. Convert Km to mol/L and report in L/(mol·s) to three significant figures.
Which comparison correctly uses the low-substrate efficiency metric and the saturation limit?
options: Enzyme B has kcat/Km = 4.00×10^7 L/(mol·s), twice enzyme A’s 2.00×10^7, so B is faster at the low 1 μM substrate concentration under matched initial-rate assumptions. Near saturation at 1000 μM, A is faster because its kcat is higher (500 vs 400 s−1). Catalytic efficiency is a low-substrate kinetic metric, not a binding-affinity measurement.
Enzyme A has the higher catalytic efficiency because its kcat is larger; kcat/Km directly measures substrate-binding affinity and predicts the rate at every substrate concentration.
Enzyme B is faster at every substrate concentration because its catalytic efficiency is higher, even when both enzymes are saturated.

questions.prompt: A synthetic pathway study isolates four perturbations. Substrate delivery falls from 8.0 to 4.0 mmol/min. A rapid AMP increase raises PFK activity per enzyme by 25% within seconds while phosphorylation and abundance stay constant. A kinase pulse raises the phosphorylated PFK fraction from 0.15 to 0.75 within 5 min at constant total abundance, with activity per enzyme increasing. Transcription induction doubles PFK abundance after 24 h while activity per enzyme remains constant. Calculate the percent change in substrate delivery, then classify each response by regulatory layer.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate 100×(after−before)/before for substrate delivery. Report as a percent to three significant figures.
Which classification matches all four controlled observations?
options: The 8.0→4.0 delivery change is substrate-supply control; the rapid AMP-linked PFK activity rise at unchanged phosphorylation/abundance is allosteric; the kinase-linked phosphorylation/activity change at fixed abundance is covalent modification; and the 24 h increase in protein amount after transcription induction is expression. Abundance alone does not identify the active fraction.
The substrate-delivery change is covalent modification, the AMP response is enzyme expression, phosphorylation is substrate supply, and the delayed protein increase is allostery.
All four observations are changes in enzyme abundance because pathway flux depends only on total protein concentration.

questions.prompt: A synthetic linear pathway A→B→C→D begins at steady state with v1=v2=v3=8.0 mM/min. A partial block lowers the B→C flux v2 to 5.0 mM/min during the initial interval, while upstream v1 remains 8.0 and no feedback or alternate route has responded yet. Calculate the initial rate of change in the B pool, then predict the immediate direction of connected pathway effects and state why later measurements may differ.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate dB/dt = vin−vout for the initial interval. Report in mM/min to three significant figures.
Which interpretation follows from the stated initial model and boundary?
options: B initially accumulates at 8.0−5.0 = 3.0 mM/min. Less material passes the inhibited B→C step, so downstream delivery falls over the following interval; later feedback, transport or alternate routes may change the response, so the initial prediction is not a complete long-term mechanism.
B immediately falls at 3.0 mM/min because vout exceeds vin, and downstream flux must rise to restore the original steady state without compensation.
B stays constant because its concentration is a pool, and the partial block cannot affect connected fluxes unless enzyme abundance changes first.

questions.prompt: A synthetic protein is modeled as a two-state folded ⇌ unfolded equilibrium at 25 °C with ΔG_unfold = +8.00 kJ/mol and RT = 2.479 kJ/mol. Calculate the folded fraction, then select the consistent equilibrium constant and stability interpretation.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate f_folded = 1/(1+Ku), with Ku = exp(−ΔG_unfold/RT). Report as a fraction to three significant figures.
Which interpretation is consistent with the stated ΔG_unfold sign and two-state model?
options: With ΔG_unfold = −RT ln Ku, Ku = exp(−8.00/2.479) ≈ 0.0397, so the folded fraction is 1/(1+Ku) ≈ 0.962. Positive ΔG_unfold favors the folded state in this two-state model.
Ku = exp(+8.00/2.479) ≈ 25.2 and 0.962 is the unfolded fraction; positive ΔG_unfold favors unfolding.
The folded fraction equals exp(−ΔG_unfold/RT) ≈ 0.0397, and the two-state equilibrium constant cannot distinguish folded from unfolded protein.

questions.prompt: In a synthetic two-state denaturation experiment, ΔG_unfold changes linearly with urea concentration across the two supplied points. Use ΔG_unfold([D]) = ΔG_H₂O − m[D] to estimate ΔG_H₂O and the midpoint C_m = ΔG_H₂O/m.

response_fields.prompt: Estimate ΔG_H₂O, the unfolding free energy extrapolated to zero denaturant. Report in kJ/mol to three significant figures.
Estimate C_m, the denaturant concentration where ΔG_unfold = 0. Report in M to three significant figures.

questions.prompt: A synthetic protein follows a two-state folded ⇌ unfolded equilibrium at 25 °C. A destabilizing substitution changes ΔG_unfold by the amount in the dataset. Calculate K_u(mutant)/K_u(WT), then select the interpretation that connects the unfolded population to proteostasis.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate K_u(mutant)/K_u(WT) from ΔΔG_unfold and RT. Report to three significant figures.
Which interpretation best follows from the two-state model?
options: A destabilizing ΔΔG_unfold raises K_u by about 25.2-fold. The mutant remains about 99.89% folded, but its unfolded population rises roughly 25-fold, increasing the load on cellular proteostasis.
A negative ΔΔG_unfold stabilizes the protein, so K_u falls by about 25-fold and fewer molecules are exposed to aggregation or degradation.
An 8 kJ/mol decrease in ΔG_unfold means about 25% of the mutant is unfolded; the folded fraction is therefore too small for chaperone capacity to matter.

questions.prompt: A synthetic initial-rate assay has three independent reactions in each of four groups. Summarize the replicate rates without pooling across either condition or substrate concentration.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the mean initial rate for the control group at [S] = 2.5 μM. Report to two decimal places.
Calculate the mean initial rate for the control group at [S] = 20 μM. Report to two decimal places.
Calculate the mean initial rate for the inhibitor group at [S] = 2.5 μM. Report to two decimal places.
Calculate the mean initial rate for the inhibitor group at [S] = 20 μM. Report to two decimal places.
Which summary preserves the experimental grouping?
options: Keep all four condition-by-concentration means separate, and report n = 3 independent reactions in each group.
Pool control and inhibitor rates at each matched substrate concentration, reporting n = 6 for each mean.
Pool the two substrate concentrations within each condition, reporting one mean per condition.

questions.prompt: A synthetic enzyme dataset was summarized with double-reciprocal fits, 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. Use the fitted slopes, intercepts and inhibitor concentration to calculate Ki and select the consistent parameter set.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate Ki for the competitive-inhibitor model. Report in μM to three significant figures.
Which Vmax, Km and inhibitor interpretation follows from the fitted slopes and intercepts?
options: Vmax is 100 μM/min in both conditions; control Km is 5 μM, inhibitor Km,app is 15 μM, α is 3, and Ki is 2 μM.
Vmax falls from 100 to 33.3 μM/min while Km stays 5 μM in both conditions; the inhibitor is purely noncompetitive.
Control Vmax is 100 μM/min and Km is 5 μM; inhibitor Km,app is 15 μM, but Ki = [I](α−1) = 8 μM.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the synthetic inhibition pattern and the quality of the candidate assay intervals. A rate is treated as initial only when substrate depletion remains below about 10% and product inhibition is negligible.

response_fields.prompt: Given the reciprocal-fit coefficients, which conclusion and method limitation are justified?
options: The unchanged y-intercept and larger slope support a competitive-inhibition pattern. The reciprocal plot can show the pattern, but magnifies low-rate errors, so untransformed nonlinear fitting is preferable for parameter estimates.
The unchanged y-intercept and larger slope prove pure noncompetitive inhibition, and the reciprocal plot is the least biased method for estimating parameters.
The larger slope shows Vmax increased while Km stayed fixed; the reciprocal transform removes measurement error at low rates.

response_fields.prompt: Which assay interval satisfies the stated initial-rate criteria?
options: Use the initial interval: 4% of substrate is consumed and no product-inhibition signal is detected. The late interval (18% consumed with a product signal) is not a trustworthy initial-rate window.
Use the late interval because larger product accumulation makes the measured rate more representative of initial velocity.
Average both intervals together; substrate depletion and product inhibition cancel when the same amount of time is sampled.

questions.prompt: A synthetic preparation has high ribose-phosphate demand relative to NADPH demand and is supplied with glycolytic intermediates. Use the stated idealized nonoxidative carbon balance to calculate pentose output, then interpret how NADP+ availability can affect the oxidative branch.

response_fields.prompt: Using the idealized net balance 2 F6P + G3P ⇌ 3 pentose phosphates, calculate the pentose-phosphate amount formed from the supplied F6P and G3P. Report in mol.
Which statement correctly links pentose demand, reversible carbon rearrangement and NADP+ availability?
options: Reversible nonoxidative rearrangement can use 2 F6P + G3P to form 3 pentose phosphates without oxidative decarboxylation. NADP+ is a G6PD substrate, so its availability can support oxidative-branch flux when G6P is available, though demand and network state also matter.
Every ribose 5-phosphate must come from oxidative glucose decarboxylation, and NADPH—not NADP+—is the substrate that accepts electrons at G6PD.
The nonoxidative rearrangement releases CO2 and produces NADPH directly; increasing NADP+ therefore blocks the oxidative branch.

questions.prompt: After nitrogen is separated from each amino acid, track the remaining carbon skeleton for alanine, aspartate, leucine and phenylalanine. Match their entry products and classify whether each can contribute net glucose carbon, ketone-body carbon, or both.

response_fields.prompt: Which mapping of the four representative amino-acid carbon skeletons is correct?
options: Alanine → pyruvate; aspartate → oxaloacetate; leucine → acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate; phenylalanine → fumarate plus acetoacetate.
Alanine → acetyl-CoA; aspartate → acetoacetate; leucine → fumarate; phenylalanine → pyruvate only.
Alanine → oxaloacetate; aspartate → acetyl-CoA; leucine → fumarate plus acetoacetate; phenylalanine → pyruvate only.

response_fields.prompt: Which glucogenic/ketogenic classification follows from those carbon products?
options: Alanine and aspartate are glucogenic; leucine is exclusively ketogenic; phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic.
Alanine and aspartate are ketogenic only; leucine is both; phenylalanine is glucogenic only.
All four are exclusively glucogenic because their carbon enters central metabolism.

questions.prompt: Interpret an alanine transamination and a separate acetyl-CoA entry into the citric acid cycle. Keep nitrogen transfer, carbon-skeleton fate and net glucose balance distinct.

response_fields.prompt: Which products keep alanine nitrogen transfer separate from its carbon-skeleton fate?
options: Alanine transfers its amino group to α-ketoglutarate, leaving pyruvate as the carbon skeleton and placing the transferred nitrogen on glutamate.
Alanine transfers its carbon skeleton to α-ketoglutarate, while its amino group becomes pyruvate.
Transamination sends both alanine carbon and nitrogen into glutamate, so no distinct carbon skeleton remains.

response_fields.prompt: Why is acetyl-CoA alone not a net glucose precursor in mammals?
options: Acetyl-CoA can enter the cycle, but complete turns do not create a net increase in oxaloacetate; carbon is released as CO₂. Labeled acetyl carbon in downstream pools does not by itself show net glucose production.
Acetyl-CoA adds a net oxaloacetate each turn, so any amino acid yielding acetyl-CoA is glucogenic.
Finding labeled acetyl carbon in a glucose precursor proves that acetyl-CoA supplied a net gain of glucose carbon.

questions.prompt: In the lesson’s simplified fed-state model, citrate export rises while ACC is active. Track how citrate supplies cytosolic acetyl-CoA and how the resulting malonyl-CoA connects synthesis to mitochondrial fatty-acid entry.

response_fields.prompt: Which statement correctly explains how exported citrate supplies cytosolic acetyl-CoA?
options: Citrate can leave the mitochondrion and ATP citrate lyase uses it to regenerate cytosolic acetyl-CoA; acetyl-CoA itself is not transported across the inner membrane in this model.
Acetyl-CoA crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane directly, while citrate remains trapped in the matrix.
Citrate export produces cytosolic malonyl-CoA without ATP citrate lyase or an acetyl-CoA intermediate.

response_fields.prompt: Which statement links ACC control, malonyl-CoA use and mitochondrial fatty-acid entry?
options: ACC converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA; citrate can activate ACC and AMPK phosphorylation inhibits it. Malonyl-CoA supplies fatty-acid synthase and inhibits CPT1, limiting long-chain acyl entry into mitochondria.
ACC consumes malonyl-CoA to make acetyl-CoA; malonyl-CoA activates CPT1 and increases mitochondrial fatty-acid entry while synthesis rises.
AMPK phosphorylation activates ACC, while citrate inhibits it; malonyl-CoA is only a storage product and does not regulate fatty-acid entry.

questions.prompt: Trace a synthetic hepatic neutral-lipid synthesis route from glycerol-3-phosphate to triacylglycerol, then connect that stored lipid to the liver’s export particle.

response_fields.prompt: Which sequence follows the glycerol-3-phosphate route to triacylglycerol?
options: Glycerol-3-phosphate is acylated to lysophosphatidic acid, then phosphatidic acid, then diacylglycerol; adding a third acyl-CoA yields triacylglycerol.
Glycerol-3-phosphate is converted directly to triacylglycerol, then loses acyl chains to form phosphatidic acid and lysophosphatidic acid.
Diacylglycerol is first deacylated to glycerol-3-phosphate, which is exported as VLDL without an acylation step.

response_fields.prompt: How does hepatic triacylglycerol storage connect to export?
options: Hepatocytes can package synthesized TAG into VLDL for export, connecting neutral-lipid synthesis/storage with a liver-derived lipoprotein route.
Hepatocytes export newly synthesized TAG only in intestinal chylomicrons, which are assembled in enterocytes.
VLDL is an intracellular storage droplet that cannot carry TAG into circulation.

questions.prompt: A synthetic tracer model assigns a fraction of lipogenic acetyl-CoA to branched-chain amino-acid carbon in two adipocyte culture states. Calculate the change, then limit the inference to the measured pool and model.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the difference between the two model-assigned fractions. Report in percentage points using the percent unit.
Which interpretation stays within the stated tracer model and carbon-balance evidence?
options: The model-assigned BCAA contribution to lipogenic acetyl-CoA is 18 percentage points higher in this differentiated-cell comparison. It does not establish a 3.25-fold increase in total BCAA oxidation, a whole-body value, or net glucose production from leucine.
The 26% label proves total BCAA oxidation increased 3.25-fold in the whole animal and that leucine supplied net glucose carbon.
Because labeled BCAA carbon appears in a lipogenic pool, leucine is glucogenic and its carbon must have passed through net glucose synthesis.

questions.prompt: A synthetic [1,2-13C2]glucose tracer model reports a ribose 5-phosphate isotopomer distribution. Calculate the fraction with one or more labels and state what the distribution does—and does not—establish about pathway flux.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the fraction of ribose isotopomers with at least one label (M+1 plus M+2). Report as a percent to three significant figures.
Which conclusion is supported by the isotopomer distribution alone?
options: Labeled carbon reached ribose in this synthetic sample, but the isotopomer fraction alone does not assign oxidative versus nonoxidative pathway flux or quantify a rate; a suitable atom-transition model and multiple measurements are needed.
A 60% labeled-ribose fraction means exactly 60% of glucose carbon passed through the oxidative PPP and gives its absolute flux.
The labeled fraction proves that 60% of ribose was made by one irreversible nonoxidative reaction and that no carbon exchange occurred.

questions.prompt: A synthetic liver-cell model supplies 5 mol of nitrogen atoms for complete disposal through the urea cycle. Calculate the stoichiometric urea amount and identify the associated energy cost, keeping ATP molecules separate from high-energy phosphate equivalents.

response_fields.prompt: Calculate the urea amount under the stated closed-balance assumption. Report in mol to three significant figures.
Which energy ledger matches the calculated urea amount?
options: Each urea contains two nitrogen atoms, so 5 mol nitrogen yields 2.50 mol urea. At 3 mol ATP molecules and 4 mol high-energy phosphate equivalents per mol urea, the load requires 7.50 mol ATP molecules and 10 mol high-energy phosphate equivalents.
The 5 mol nitrogen load forms 5 mol urea, requiring 15 mol ATP molecules and 20 mol high-energy phosphate equivalents.
The load forms 2.50 mol urea, requiring 10 mol ATP molecules and 7.50 mol high-energy phosphate equivalents.
